newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Two Qatari on trial in Bahrian for spying.
newsitem.headline: Two Qatari on trial in Bahrian for spying.

text.p: Bahrain on Wednesday opened an espionage trial of two Qataris who could face execution or long prison terms if convicted, an official and a lawyer said.
"Bahrain's State Security Court today started trying the two Qataris in the presence of their families," the official told Reuters.

Bahrain said on Monday the two accused, a man and a woman, had confessed before an investigating judge to spying for Doha. They were named as Fahad Hamad Abdullah al-Baker and Salwa Jassim Mohammed Fakhri.
Qatar has denied they were spies.
"We expect the trial will not be long if all the evidence is available...just two or three sessions," a source close to the trial said.
He declined to say what sentences they could face, but a lawyer told Reuters "It depends on the charges. They could face execution or a long term in prison".
Judgments of Bahrain's State Security Court, set up this year to accelerate trials of prisoners connected with anti-government unrest, are final - defendants have no right of appeal.

The spy charges have added to tensions between Bahrain and Qatar, already at loggerheads over a cluster of barren but potentially rich reefs, sandbanks and Gulf islands controlled by Bahrain since the 1930s.

By putting the two Qataris on trial, Bahrain has raised the stakes in its dispute with Qatar, a fellow member of the Gulf Cooperation Council that also includes Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, United Arab Emirates and Oman.
A Qatari foreign ministry official on Wednesday said, "We are shocked at the news."

"We have repeatedly told Bahrain that the Qataris are not spies. They were lost in Bahrain. We had asked the Bahraini authorities to locate them and now we find they have been arrested. We have no intelligence to gather about Bahrain," he said.

Bahraini newspapers on Wednesday quoted an interior ministry spokesman as saying the two suspects had been charged with gathering intelligence for the Doha government in an effort to undermine Bahrain's security.
They are also accused of accepting money from Qatar.
Bahrain has already expressed its anger with Qatar by refusing to attend a Gulf Arab summit to be held in Doha on Saturday, saying Qatar had behaved in an "unfriendly manner".

Doha newspapers have said the spying charges were intended to undermine the summit and abort an initiative by Qatar's Emir Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani to visit Bahrain to try to persuade it not to boycott the summit.
"We feel Bahrain is trying to undermine the GCC summit by levelling spying charges against Qatar. It's not in the brotherly spirit," said the Qatari foreign ministry official.
